summary: Describes how forward error correction codes can efficiently provide or augment reliability for one-to-many multicast transport. A key advantage is that the same repair packets can fix different loss patterns at different receivers. It describes classes of codes and some of their basic properties.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3453 explains how extra coded packets can help multicast receivers recover different lost packets. It describes several kinds of forward error correction and ways they can support reliable delivery.

questions: forward error correction multicast loss repair
subtitle: How forward error correction can repair different packet losses for multicast receivers.

tldr.problem: Retransmission feedback can scale poorly to many multicast receivers, while a repeated data carousel makes receivers wait for another round to recover losses.
tldr.mechanism: Forward Error Correction (FEC) creates encoding symbols so a receiver can reconstruct source data from enough received symbols, including symbols that repair different losses at different receivers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes FEC code families and ways to use them for reliable multicast. It is an Informational overview, not a protocol specification.

facts.value: Less than 5% for k in the tens to hundreds of thousands

today: RFC 3453 is an Informational document published in December 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it provides background on FEC for reliable multicast rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Why Use FEC for Multicast
sections.content:
Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) asks a sender to retransmit lost packets. With very many receivers, requests can overwhelm the sender, require a return channel, and waste time or bandwidth when receivers lose different packets. A data carousel avoids feedback by repeating the object, but a receiver may wait for another full round to receive a lost packet.

Forward Error Correction (FEC) can add redundant information so receivers recover losses without requesting particular packets. For IP multicast, the RFC focuses on erasure codes because network or transport layers discard corrupted packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast receivers can lose different packets, making individual retransmission requests difficult to coordinate. FEC sends coded information that can help receivers recover without requesting each lost packet.

sections.title: Source Symbols and Encoding Symbols
sections.content:
An encoder takes k equal-length source symbols and creates encoding symbols of the same length. Each packet carries enough information to identify its encoding symbols. Ideally, a decoder can recover the original k source symbols from any k encoding symbols.

A block code creates n encoding symbols from k source symbols; a systematic code includes the source symbols plus n-k redundant symbols. Some practical codes need more than k received symbols, which the RFC calls reception overhead. Codes can be designed for small or large blocks, or to create more symbols as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An encoder creates original and redundant symbols, and each packet identifies the symbols it carries. A receiver collects enough distinct symbols to reconstruct the original data.

sections.title: Ways to Apply FEC
sections.content:
A protocol can combine FEC with ARQ: receivers report how many symbols they lack in each block, and the sender transmits enough redundant symbols for the largest reported loss. One set of redundant symbols can help several receivers even when they lost different source symbols.

An FEC data carousel repeatedly sends encoding symbols, allowing a receiver to join during a transmission round and recover after receiving enough symbols. With expandable codes, the sender can instead generate new encoding symbols as needed. A sender can also decide in advance how many symbols to send once, as in a streaming protocol that divides its data into objects.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC can work with receiver feedback, repeated transmissions, or a planned one-time transmission. The same redundant symbols can help multiple receivers with different loss patterns.

sections.title: Families of FEC Codes
sections.content:
A simple XOR parity symbol can recover one missing source symbol. Small block codes, including Reed-Solomon codes, can recover from any k of n symbols but become expensive at larger block sizes; the RFC gives values below 256 as an example of small k and n.

Tornado codes support large blocks and need a small amount of reception overhead; for n = 2k, the RFC cites 5-10%. LT codes are expandable and can generate symbols from random encoding-symbol identifiers. For k in the tens to hundreds of thousands, the RFC cites reception overhead below 5%.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple parity can repair one lost symbol, while other code families handle larger blocks or generate symbols as needed. Each family trades processing cost against how many symbols a receiver must collect.

sections.title: Identifying Symbols of Different Lengths
sections.content:
Block FEC codes use equal-length source symbols. To handle source symbols of different lengths, the RFC describes padding each symbol with zeroes to the maximum length and adding its original length before encoding. Each padded symbol then has the same length.

After decoding, the receiver reads each stored length and extracts the original number of bytes. Packets also need identifiers such as a block number and an encoding-symbol ID so receivers can distinguish symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: For a block code, shorter symbols are padded to match the longest one, and their original lengths are recorded. After recovery, the receiver uses those lengths to restore the original symbols.

sections.title: Authenticating Encoding Symbols
sections.content:
FEC itself adds no security concerns compared with sending the same data without FEC. However, a malicious sender can inject corrupted encoding symbols, which may cause a receiver to reconstruct a corrupted object and discard the transfer.

The RFC discusses screening source addresses but notes they can be spoofed. It recommends packet authentication, such as TESLA, so receivers can discard unauthenticated packets and reconstruct the object from authenticated symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: False encoding symbols can make a receiver reconstruct damaged data. Authentication can help receivers reject symbols that did not come from an accepted sender.
